definition: Chronology means the order in which events actually happened in time, or an account that sets events out in that order.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word chronology. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know chronology should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: No two biographers agree on the chronology of the poet's lost years — the letters are undated, and the landlords kept no books.
A sequence is a weaker claim than a chronology: it promises only that one item follows another, on any basis at all, while a chronology commits every event to its real place in time.
A timetable is stricter than a chronology, nailing each entry to an exact clock reading; a chronology fixes the true order of events without demanding the minute of every one.

A timeline is the graphic form: events plotted along a drawn line, often for a project still ahead. Chronology is the underlying time-order itself, and it belongs to events that have actually happened, whether or not anyone draws them.

A chronicle is a written record kept as events unfold — a monastery's year-by-year annals. Chronology is the time-order itself, whether or not anyone wrote it down; you can reconstruct a chronology centuries later, but a chronicle is set down as things happen.

The shoebox held ninety photographs of the farm, none of them labeled, spanning what looked like half a century.
Before the family could mount an exhibit for the reunion, someone had to work out the chronology — not just group the pictures, but set them in the order the years actually ran.
Cousin Ada did it with details: the barn's roofline changed in one storm, the oak by the gate thickened, license plates on the trucks changed style.
A photo with the old roof and the young oak had to come early; one with solar panels could only come last.
When she finished, the wall told a single story from homestead to harvest festival, and even the oldest cousins learned which fire, flood, and wedding had truly come first.
